interest: Marine machinery, entire — boilers, superheat, gearing, and above all the shore-plant research program that broke each generation at Haslar before it went to sea. This is PROCESS under §8's premise clause; the lead is in the failure rate.

⚠ THE COMPARATOR IS OBSCURE AND IS NAMED HERE BECAUSE THE BAND CANNOT BE READ WITHOUT IT. Royal Navy production practice was 250 psi at Nelson in 1927 and 300 psi through the 1930s destroyers, and the RN did not reach 600 psi in service until the Daring class of 1952 — against which this ladder would be +18 and indefensible. But HMS ACHERON WENT TO SEA ON 12 OCTOBER 1931 AT 500 PSI AND 750 °F, and her plant's failure is precisely what 'convinced the Admiralty not to continue with experiments with high boiler pressures.' Against Acheron the ladder is 1927 at 400 psi (+4), 1930 at 500 psi (+1) and 1934 at 600 psi / 450 °C (+3 on USS Somers, 1937, at 600 psi / 850 °F). ⚠ FISHER'S GHOST IS THE WORLD IN WHICH ACHERON WORKED, and every rung is inside the interest band.

the hull form that spends it: THIRTY-SIX KNOTS ON A FULLY ARMORED FIFTY-THOUSAND-TON HULL, held by battle line, cruiser and carrier alike from 1929 on. That combination is the only figure in this file with no historical analogue, and it is bought entirely out of the machinery lead above.

THE HEAVY LINE TOPS OUT AT 18 INCHES AND CLAIMS NOTHING. The Mark III is the 1917 bore relined — a gun Britain actually built, proofed and fired — and its 1,510 kg shell is the 1917 shell weight, below the Japanese 46 cm Type 94's 1,460 kg only in caliber and above nothing at all in energy. This ladder buys knots; it has never once bought a caliber.
supporting: Asdic, which is genuinely the best in the world and which this fleet has almost nothing to fit. ⚠ Type 112 was at sea in 1920 and Type 114 in 1922, so a 1926 set at 1,800 m reliable and 3,200 m in good conditions is AT the period ceiling and not past it; depth determination in 1941 is +2 on the real Type 147 of May 1943. The chemical range recorder sits in the 1934 generation, against a real Type 124 of 1934.
Heavy-gun fire control: the tower, the table, the stable element, and aircraft spot correction into the plot

The abeam refueling rig, without which the machinery lead stops at the dockyard wall. ⚠ IT IS A LAG, NOT A LEAD: Nimitz and Dinger had an abeam rig working on USS Maumee in 1916 and the US Navy fueled 34 destroyers abeam in 1917, while the real Royal Navy abandoned the method in 1911 and relearned it from the Americans in 1943–44. Britain having it in 1930 is THIRTEEN YEARS BEHIND the United States.
par: Heavy guns and their mountings. ⚠ [uk22gun] SITS AT OR BELOW ITS REAL COMPARATOR ON EVERY FIGURE: every figure is at or below the real 16-inch/45 Mark I — 929 kg at 788 m/s, and 34,300 m against the real gun's 34,750–36,375 m — and the guns and mountings were ON ORDER FROM 24 OCTOBER 1921 for the G3s. The 1927 service date is an artifact of the cancellation this scenario reverses. [uk27gun] is likewise conservative: no British 16-inch/50 ever existed, and against the American 16-inch/50 Mark 2 proved on 8 April 1918 at 853 m/s, a 1927 gun at 815 m/s is nine years late and slower.

⚠ THE TUBE COUNT ON A TORPEDO MOUNTING IS A LAYOUT AND NOT A PERFORMANCE FIGURE. The real Royal Navy went triple in 1918, quadruple in 1930 (HMS Active) and quintuple in 1939 (HMS Jervis); this catalog is quadruple in 1925 and quintuple in 1933. Diameter, train rate, gyro-angle firing and the zero reload stowage are all par, and the reloads are zero because the real ones were.

⚠ AND THE DUAL-PURPOSE SECONDARY IS THE SAME SPLIT, STATED BECAUSE IT IS THE LARGEST DATE LEAD IN THIS FILE. [uk32sec]'s ballistics are the real 4.5-inch/45 QF Mark I to three figures — 24.95 kg at 746 m/s to 18,970 m, 12,500 m ceiling, 12 rpm — and that gun entered service in 1938, six years after this one. What runs deep is the ENCLOSED DUAL-PURPOSE BASE-RING MOUNTING, which is mounting architecture under the premise clause. ⚠ THE PROOF IT IS NOT SMUGGLING A PERFORMANCE CLAIM IS THE WEIGHT: 43 t against the real BD Mark II's 38.6, so this navy's mounting is HEAVIER than the article it is drawn from. Eight classes carry it and its code year cannot move without redrawing four as-launched fits.

The multiple pom-pom. ⚠ NOT COLD: the real octuple was in service at the end of 1930 at 96–98 rpm a barrel on 140-round feeds and 16 tons, which is this row exactly, three years early. Britain's anti-aircraft coldness is the ABSENCE of a director until 1938 and of any second mounting in any year — not the gun. Its shell is the real high-velocity round, 0.82 kg at 732 m/s.

ARMOR, which is par because it is not invented at all: the 356 mm belt, the 203 mm magazine deck, the 356 mm barbettes and the 432 mm faces are the G3 design of 1921 to the inch, and all four classes carry them unaltered. A navy that stops developing armor and keeps building the same scheme for fourteen years ends the period behind — but nothing here is a claim.
cold: Anti-aircraft gunnery as a SYSTEM, for thirteen of the fourteen years — one mounting, no director until 1938, no second weapon in any year. ⚠ THE GUN ITSELF IS PAR, and ⚠ THE ANSWER EXISTS AND IS INCORRIGIBLE, WHO IS 8 PERCENT BUILT WHEN PLAY BEGINS. A navy whose air defense is a design study is cold whatever the design study says.

Naval aviation's ORGANIZATION, and only the organization — no fighter direction, no radar to vector from, no deck park, interception on sight from a deck alert, and air groups of 51 on decks that could work 70. ⚠ THE AIRFRAMES ARE PAR AND NOT IN THIS BAND: a 1936 scout dive-bomber at 365 km/h against a real Skua of 1938 at 362, a 1937 torpedo monoplane at 350 against the Devastator of the same year at 332, and a 1938 single-seat fleet fighter at 470 against an F3F biplane at 425. ⚠ THERE IS STILL NO AERO-ENGINE LINE IN THIS CATALOG AND THERE NEVER WAS ONE: Britain has no engine SKU, because the Admiralty buys airplanes and not engines, and a British aircraft's powerplant is stated on its own sheet.

Trade defense entire — no escort, no sloop, no corvette, no reserve, in any year. ⚠ AND THE DEPTH CHARGE IS THE MEASURE OF IT: the 1922 charge is the wartime Type D at 190 kg with 130 kg of explosive, and the 1937 charge is 191 kg with 132 kg. Fifteen years and it did not grow.
⚠ THE STRONGEST FORM OF THIS BAND IS AGAIN AN ABSENCE: there is no escort line, no sloop line and no corvette line in this catalog, because there was no program.
calibration.notes: Britain bought ONE thing with fifteen years and paid for it in every category that would have mattered later, and the one thing is not armor: she drew a well-protected capital ship in 1921 and then built it four times, changing not one plate of the scheme. The cold bands are where the money did not go, and the money went into ten capital hulls in fourteen years. Every generation in this file is checked against the best real-world article at any date in the window, and the only line that runs deep is the machinery — which is process, and whose comparator is HMS Acheron, named in the interest band.

A DESIGN STANDARD, NOT A SWAPPABLE ARTICLE: a hull receives the generation current on the day her keel is laid and keeps it for life, and the only way to change it is to cut the ship open. Britain has done that three times in fourteen years. Every other navy's Machinery row is a menu; Britain's is a birth certificate. The lead is a PROCESS — full-scale shore boiler rooms at Haslar that failed on land, on the Admiralty's own money — which is why nobody has copied it.

The Portland school produces operators the fleet cannot billet and tables the fleet does not exercise, and the Anti-Submarine Division's annual report has said so in the same three paragraphs since 1929.

The Torpedo Establishment was given the airframe's figures and told to work backwards from them, which is the reverse of how every other weapon in this catalog was specified and shows in the result. THE FLEET AIR ARM'S REAL WEAPON IS NOT THIS ONE: it is the wireless set in the observer's cockpit and the fall of shot it corrects.

The doctrine is defensive and unimaginative: a declared area, a published warning and a field somebody else's merchant ships have to go round.
